title: Introduction and OS foundations
source: SC2005 lecture slides, tutorial material, lab manuals and quiz screenshots.
context: Introduction and OS foundations: practise both conceptual explanations and exam-style traces/calculations.

qs.stem: The primary role of an operating system is to:
qs.correct: act as an intermediary between users/applications and hardware
qs.why: The correct answer is B: act as an intermediary between users/applications and hardware.
options: act as an intermediary between users/applications and hardware

qs.stem: Which is not one of the four broad components of a computer system?
qs.correct: Compiler optimisations only
qs.why: The correct answer is D: Compiler optimisations only.

qs.stem: The kernel is best described as:
qs.correct: the core OS program that remains ready to handle requests and hardware events
qs.why: The correct answer is B: the core OS program that remains ready to handle requests and hardware events.
options: the core OS program that remains ready to handle requests and hardware events

qs.stem: A simple batch system can waste CPU time when the current job:
qs.correct: waits for I/O
qs.why: The correct answer is B: waits for I/O.

qs.stem: A real-time system is characterised mainly by:
qs.correct: fixed timing constraints and deadlines
qs.why: The correct answer is B: fixed timing constraints and deadlines.

qs.stem: Multiprogramming improves CPU utilisation primarily by:
qs.correct: running another ready job while one job waits for I/O
qs.why: The correct answer is B: running another ready job while one job waits for I/O.
options: running another ready job while one job waits for I/O

qs.stem: Which OS function chooses among ready jobs for the CPU?
qs.correct: CPU scheduling
qs.why: The correct answer is B: CPU scheduling.

qs.stem: In a tightly coupled multiprocessor system, processors commonly communicate through:
qs.correct: shared memory
qs.why: The correct answer is A: shared memory.

qs.stem: The main focus of a desktop OS is generally:
qs.correct: user convenience and responsiveness
qs.why: The correct answer is A: user convenience and responsiveness.
options: guaranteeing every task a hard deadline

qs.stem: A device controller usually:
qs.correct: controls a device and has a local buffer
qs.why: The correct answer is B: controls a device and has a local buffer.
options: controls a device and has a local buffer

qs.stem: The goals of convenience and efficient hardware use can conflict because:
qs.correct: sophisticated allocation may require information and overhead that reduce simplicity
qs.why: The correct answer is B: sophisticated allocation may require information and overhead that reduce simplicity.
options: sophisticated allocation may require information and overhead that reduce simplicity

qs.stem: A CPU and an I/O device can operate concurrently because:
qs.correct: the device controller can transfer data through its buffer while the CPU executes
qs.why: The correct answer is A: the device controller can transfer data through its buffer while the CPU executes.
options: the device controller can transfer data through its buffer while the CPU executes
the CPU becomes part of the disk

qs.stem: Which combination best explains why multiprocessors can be more reliable?
qs.correct: redundancy and the possibility of continued service after one component fails
qs.why: The correct answer is A: redundancy and the possibility of continued service after one component fails.
options: redundancy and the possibility of continued service after one component fails

qs.stem: A handheld OS must particularly account for:
qs.correct: limited memory, processing power and display area
qs.why: The correct answer is B: limited memory, processing power and display area.
options: limited memory, processing power and display area

qs.stem: In a time-sharing system, swapping is used chiefly to:
qs.correct: keep several jobs available and support interactive users
qs.why: The correct answer is A: keep several jobs available and support interactive users.
options: keep several jobs available and support interactive users

qs.stem: An embedded controller must react within a deadline, share one CPU among multiple activities, and protect device state. Which OS design concern is most central?
qs.correct: combining predictable scheduling, interrupt handling and protection under resource constraints
qs.why: The correct answer is B: combining predictable scheduling, interrupt handling and protection under resource constraints.
options: combining predictable scheduling, interrupt handling and protection under resource constraints
replacing all interrupts with polling only
maximising virtual address size regardless of timing

openEnded.prompt: Define an operating system and state its two broad goals.
openEnded.key: intermediary between users/applications and hardware; user convenience; efficient hardware utilisation/resource allocation.

openEnded.prompt: Explain how a simple batch system differs from a multiprogrammed/time-sharing system.
openEnded.key: one job vs several in memory; automatic job sequencing vs interactive communication; CPU idle during I/O vs another job can run; need for memory/CPU/I/O scheduling.

openEnded.prompt: Explain why OS abstractions, policies and mechanisms are useful, and give one example of each.
openEnded.key: abstraction hides complexity; policy decides what should happen; mechanism implements how; examples such as files/CPU scheduling policy/context-switch mechanism.

openEnded.prompt: Design a high-level OS strategy for a medical embedded controller that must meet deadlines but also log data and support updates.
openEnded.key: hard/soft real-time distinction; priority/deadline scheduling; bounded interrupt and I/O paths; memory protection; isolation/update recovery; logging must not block critical work; explain trade-offs.

title: Processes and threads
source: SC2005 lecture slides, tutorial material, lab manuals and quiz screenshots.
context: Processes and threads: practise both conceptual explanations and exam-style traces/calculations.

qs.stem: A process is:
qs.correct: a program in execution
qs.why: The correct answer is A: a program in execution.

qs.stem: A process waiting for an I/O completion is in the:
qs.correct: waiting/blocked state
qs.why: The correct answer is B: waiting/blocked state.

qs.stem: The PCB normally stores:
qs.correct: process state, program counter and registers among other information
qs.why: The correct answer is B: process state, program counter and registers among other information.
options: process state, program counter and registers among other information

qs.stem: A context switch requires the OS to:
qs.correct: save the old process context and load the new one
qs.why: The correct answer is A: save the old process context and load the new one.
options: save the old process context and load the new one

qs.stem: A thread is best viewed as:
qs.correct: a unit of execution within a process
qs.why: The correct answer is A: a unit of execution within a process.
options: a unit of execution within a process

qs.stem: A process in the ready state is:
qs.correct: able to execute but waiting for CPU allocation
qs.why: The correct answer is B: able to execute but waiting for CPU allocation.
options: able to execute but waiting for CPU allocation

qs.stem: The short-term scheduler selects from the:
qs.correct: ready queue
qs.why: The correct answer is B: ready queue.

qs.stem: The long-term scheduler mainly controls:
qs.correct: the degree of multiprogramming by admitting jobs to memory
qs.why: The correct answer is A: the degree of multiprogramming by admitting jobs to memory.
options: the degree of multiprogramming by admitting jobs to memory

qs.stem: The medium-term scheduler is associated with:
qs.correct: swapping partially executed processes out and back in
qs.why: The correct answer is A: swapping partially executed processes out and back in.
options: swapping partially executed processes out and back in

qs.stem: If a parent calls `wait()` after creating a child, the parent generally:
qs.correct: waits for child termination/status
qs.why: The correct answer is A: waits for child termination/status.

qs.stem: A context switch is overhead because during the switch:
qs.correct: no useful user-process work is performed
qs.why: The correct answer is A: no useful user-process work is performed.
options: no useful user-process work is performed
the new process cannot ever run

qs.stem: In a many-to-one user-thread model, a blocking system call by one user thread can:
qs.correct: block the entire process because the kernel sees one schedulable thread
qs.why: The correct answer is A: block the entire process because the kernel sees one schedulable thread.
options: block the entire process because the kernel sees one schedulable thread

qs.stem: If a child performs `exec` after `fork`, the usual effect is that it:
qs.correct: replaces its process image with a new program
qs.why: The correct answer is A: replaces its process image with a new program.
options: replaces its process image with a new program

qs.stem: A zombie process is one that:
qs.correct: has exited but remains in the process table until its status is collected
qs.why: The correct answer is B: has exited but remains in the process table until its status is collected.
options: has exited but remains in the process table until its status is collected

qs.stem: On one core with preemptive Round Robin, when a quantum expires, the running process normally moves to:
qs.correct: ready, unless it has terminated or blocked
qs.why: The correct answer is A: ready, unless it has terminated or blocked.
options: ready, unless it has terminated or blocked

qs.stem: A parent creates a child at t=0; the child immediately sends a blocking IPC message at t=6; the parent’s CPU quantum expires at t=7. Assuming the child was made ready by the send and the scheduler runs immediately, which event must be true?
qs.correct: the child can enter the ready queue before t=7 and may be selected at the next scheduling opportunity
qs.why: The correct answer is B: the child can enter the ready queue before t=7 and may be selected at the next scheduling opportunity.
options: the child cannot run until the parent exits
the child can enter the ready queue before t=7 and may be selected at the next scheduling opportunity
the parent remains running despite blocking
`fork` makes both processes share one PCB

openEnded.prompt: Draw the five basic process states and explain the ready-to-running and running-to-waiting transitions.
openEnded.key: new, ready, running, waiting, terminated; scheduler dispatches ready→running; I/O/event request causes running→waiting.

openEnded.prompt: Explain the contents of a PCB and why each of the program counter, registers and memory-management information is needed during a context switch.
openEnded.key: identify fields; PC resumes next instruction; registers restore execution state; base/limit or equivalent protects/translates memory; state and scheduling data choose/resume process.

openEnded.prompt: Compare long-, medium- and short-term schedulers in trigger frequency, input/output and purpose.
openEnded.key: long-term disk→memory and admission, infrequent; short-term ready queue→CPU, frequent; medium-term swap out/in under load; degree of multiprogramming.

openEnded.prompt: Analyse a `fork`/`wait`/IPC process tree in which the parent and child have different CPU quanta and one blocks on receive. State possible process-state transitions and explain why exact execution order may be nondeterministic.
openEnded.key: separate PCBs/address spaces; scheduler/preemption; blocking receive; wake-up on send; parent may wait or run; race/order depends on timing and queue policy.

title: CPU scheduling and algorithms
source: SC2005 lecture slides, tutorial material, lab manuals and quiz screenshots.
context: CPU scheduling and algorithms: practise both conceptual explanations and exam-style traces/calculations.

qs.stem: FCFS scheduling is normally:
qs.correct: nonpreemptive
qs.why: The correct answer is A: nonpreemptive.

qs.stem: Round Robin is defined by a:
qs.correct: time quantum
qs.why: The correct answer is A: time quantum.

qs.stem: SJF chooses the process with the smallest predicted:
qs.correct: CPU burst
qs.why: The correct answer is A: CPU burst.

qs.stem: Throughput is the number of processes completed per:
qs.correct: unit time
qs.why: The correct answer is A: unit time.

qs.stem: Response time ends when a process:
qs.correct: first enters running
qs.why: The correct answer is A: first enters running.

qs.stem: FCFS’s convoy effect means:
qs.correct: short jobs wait behind a long job
qs.why: The correct answer is A: short jobs wait behind a long job.
options: short jobs wait behind a long job
every job has the same burst

qs.stem: SRTF is the preemptive version of:
qs.correct: SJF
qs.why: The correct answer is A: SJF.

qs.stem: Increasing a Round Robin quantum until it is very large makes RR approach:
qs.correct: FCFS
qs.why: The correct answer is A: FCFS.

qs.stem: Waiting time is calculated as turnaround time minus:
qs.correct: CPU bursts and I/O/event-wait time
qs.why: The correct answer is A: CPU bursts and I/O/event-wait time.

qs.stem: A preemptive scheduler may take the CPU from a running process:
qs.correct: before it voluntarily blocks or terminates
qs.why: The correct answer is A: before it voluntarily blocks or terminates.
options: before it voluntarily blocks or terminates

qs.stem: P1, P2, P3 arrive at 0 with burst lengths 8, 4, 2. Nonpreemptive SJF’s average waiting time is:
qs.why: order P3,P2,P1; waits 0,2,6

qs.stem: For FCFS order P1(5), P2(3), P3(2), all at 0, the average waiting time is:
qs.why: The correct answer is A: 13/3.

qs.stem: With RR quantum 2 and ready queue P1(5), P2(3), both at 0, after P1’s first slice the next process is:
qs.correct: P2
qs.why: The correct answer is A: P2.

qs.stem: A scheduler that prioritises short jobs minimises average waiting time under the standard assumptions because:
qs.correct: completing short bursts earlier reduces time imposed on later jobs
qs.why: The correct answer is A: completing short bursts earlier reduces time imposed on later jobs.
options: completing short bursts earlier reduces time imposed on later jobs

qs.stem: On a two-core system, CPU utilisation is total busy core-time divided by:
qs.correct: elapsed time × 2
qs.why: The correct answer is A: elapsed time × 2.

qs.stem: P1 arrives at 0 with burst 7; P2 at 2 with burst 3; P3 at 4 with burst 1. Under SRTF, which execution sequence is correct (ignoring switch cost)?

openEnded.prompt: Define turnaround, waiting and response time.
openEnded.key: admission/arrival to termination; time in ready queue; admission/arrival to first running.

openEnded.prompt: Compute the FCFS and nonpreemptive-SJF schedules and average waiting time for P1=6, P2=2, P3=4, all arriving at 0.
openEnded.key: FCFS order P1,P2,P3, waits 0,6,8, average 14/3; SJF order P2,P3,P1, waits 0,2,6, average 8/3.

openEnded.prompt: Explain the trade-off when choosing a Round Robin quantum.
openEnded.key: small quantum improves response/fairness but increases context-switch overhead; large quantum reduces overhead but approaches FCFS and harms response; workload and switch cost matter.

openEnded.prompt: Given an arrival/burst table, compare FCFS, SJF, SRTF and RR, showing Gantt charts, waiting/turnaround/response times, and one fairness/starvation observation.
openEnded.key: correct event-by-event schedule; definitions and arithmetic; explain preemption on arrivals; identify SJF starvation risk and RR fairness/overhead.

title: Process synchronization
source: SC2005 lecture slides, tutorial material, lab manuals and quiz screenshots.
context: Process synchronization: practise both conceptual explanations and exam-style traces/calculations.

qs.stem: A race condition occurs when the result depends on:
qs.correct: the timing/interleaving of concurrent accesses
qs.why: The correct answer is A: the timing/interleaving of concurrent accesses.

qs.stem: The part of a program accessing shared data is the:
qs.correct: critical section
qs.why: The correct answer is A: critical section.

qs.stem: Mutual exclusion means:
qs.correct: at most one process is in a critical section at a time
qs.why: The correct answer is A: at most one process is in a critical section at a time.
options: at most one process is in a critical section at a time

qs.stem: A semaphore wait operation generally:
qs.correct: decrements/claims a permit and may block
qs.why: The correct answer is A: decrements/claims a permit and may block.
options: decrements/claims a permit and may block

qs.stem: A binary semaphore used for mutual exclusion is commonly initialised to:
qs.why: The correct answer is A: 1.

qs.stem: The three classic critical-section requirements are:
qs.correct: mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting
qs.why: The correct answer is A: mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting.
options: mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting

qs.stem: In a bounded buffer, `empty` counts:
qs.correct: unused slots
qs.why: The correct answer is A: unused slots.

qs.stem: A producer should normally wait for `empty` before entering the buffer’s critical update because:
qs.correct: it must not insert into a full buffer
qs.why: The correct answer is A: it must not insert into a full buffer.
options: it must not insert into a full buffer
it must avoid all CPU use

qs.stem: A mutex lock is released by:
qs.correct: the owner after leaving the critical section
qs.why: The correct answer is A: the owner after leaving the critical section.
options: the owner after leaving the critical section
any unrelated process at any time

qs.stem: A monitor provides:
qs.correct: mutual exclusion around its procedures plus condition synchronisation
qs.why: The correct answer is A: mutual exclusion around its procedures plus condition synchronisation.
options: mutual exclusion around its procedures plus condition synchronisation

qs.stem: If a process executes `wait(mutex)` twice without a matching signal and mutex starts at 1, it will most likely:
qs.correct: block on the second wait
qs.why: The correct answer is A: block on the second wait.

qs.stem: In a bounded-buffer solution, the usual semaphore wait order `wait(empty); wait(mutex)` prevents:
qs.correct: a producer holding the mutex while waiting for space, which could block consumers from freeing space
qs.why: The correct answer is A: a producer holding the mutex while waiting for space, which could block consumers from freeing space.
options: a producer holding the mutex while waiting for space, which could block consumers from freeing space

qs.stem: If two increments are implemented as read–modify–write and interleave, the final value can lose an update because:
qs.correct: both processes can read the same old value
qs.why: The correct answer is A: both processes can read the same old value.
options: both processes can read the same old value

qs.stem: Busy waiting differs from blocking because a busy-waiting process:
qs.correct: repeatedly checks while consuming CPU
qs.why: The correct answer is A: repeatedly checks while consuming CPU.

qs.stem: A correct lock-free-looking algorithm that violates bounded waiting may cause:
qs.correct: starvation
qs.why: The correct answer is A: starvation.

qs.stem: Producer code is `wait(mutex); wait(empty); insert(); signal(empty); signal(mutex)`, consumer code is `wait(mutex); wait(full); remove(); signal(full); signal(mutex)`. If the buffer is full, what can happen?
qs.correct: producer holds mutex waiting for empty while consumer cannot acquire mutex to remove, causing deadlock
qs.why: The correct answer is A: producer holds mutex waiting for empty while consumer cannot acquire mutex to remove, causing deadlock.
options: producer holds mutex waiting for empty while consumer cannot acquire mutex to remove, causing deadlock
only the consumer starves but never deadlocks

openEnded.prompt: Explain race condition and critical section using a shared counter.
openEnded.key: concurrent read–modify–write; different interleavings yield different final counts; counter update is critical section.

openEnded.prompt: Write semaphore pseudocode for a bounded buffer of size N and explain `empty`, `full` and `mutex`.
openEnded.key: producer waits empty/mutex, inserts, signals mutex/full; consumer waits full/mutex, removes, signals mutex/empty; initial values N, 0, 1.

openEnded.prompt: Show how incorrect semaphore order can deadlock the bounded-buffer solution.
openEnded.key: producer/consumer each hold mutex then wait on unavailable resource; opposite party needs mutex to create that resource; demonstrate cycle; correct order releases/claims counting semaphore before mutex.

openEnded.prompt: Compare mutex, binary semaphore, counting semaphore and monitor for a shared resource with multiple conditions.
openEnded.key: ownership vs permit semantics; counting capacity; monitor encapsulation and condition variables; waking semantics; misuse and deadlock risks; justify a design.

title: Deadlocks and starvation
source: SC2005 lecture slides, tutorial material, lab manuals and quiz screenshots.
context: Deadlocks and starvation: practise both conceptual explanations and exam-style traces/calculations.

qs.stem: A deadlock is a state where processes:
qs.correct: wait forever for events/resources held by one another
qs.why: The correct answer is A: wait forever for events/resources held by one another.
options: wait forever for events/resources held by one another

qs.stem: Which is a necessary deadlock condition?
qs.correct: mutual exclusion
qs.why: The correct answer is A: mutual exclusion.

qs.stem: Hold-and-wait means a process:
qs.correct: holds at least one resource while waiting for another
qs.why: The correct answer is A: holds at least one resource while waiting for another.
options: holds at least one resource while waiting for another

qs.stem: Starvation means:
qs.correct: indefinite postponement while other processes continue to progress
qs.why: The correct answer is A: indefinite postponement while other processes continue to progress.
options: indefinite postponement while other processes continue to progress
all processes are blocked in a cycle necessarily

qs.stem: A resource-allocation graph can represent:
qs.correct: processes, resources and request/assignment edges
qs.why: The correct answer is A: processes, resources and request/assignment edges.

qs.stem: The four Coffman conditions are mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and:
qs.correct: circular wait
qs.why: The correct answer is A: circular wait.

qs.stem: Deadlock prevention works by:
qs.correct: denying at least one necessary condition
qs.why: The correct answer is A: denying at least one necessary condition.
options: denying at least one necessary condition

qs.stem: A safe state is one in which:
qs.correct: there exists an order allowing all processes to finish with available resources
qs.why: The correct answer is A: there exists an order allowing all processes to finish with available resources.
options: there exists an order allowing all processes to finish with available resources

qs.stem: Banker’s algorithm grants a request only if the resulting state is:
qs.correct: safe
qs.why: The correct answer is A: safe.

qs.stem: Deadlock detection differs from prevention because detection:
qs.correct: allows deadlock to occur and then searches for it
qs.why: The correct answer is A: allows deadlock to occur and then searches for it.
options: allows deadlock to occur and then searches for it

qs.stem: If P1 holds R1 and requests R2 while P2 holds R2 and requests R1, the graph contains:
qs.correct: a cycle and a deadlock under single-instance resources
qs.why: The correct answer is A: a cycle and a deadlock under single-instance resources.
options: a cycle and a deadlock under single-instance resources

qs.stem: A safe sequence is best described as:
qs.correct: an ordering in which each process can obtain its remaining need and release resources
qs.why: The correct answer is A: an ordering in which each process can obtain its remaining need and release resources.
options: an ordering in which each process can obtain its remaining need and release resources

qs.stem: Requiring processes to request all resources before execution can prevent hold-and-wait but may cause:
qs.correct: low utilisation and possible starvation
qs.why: The correct answer is A: low utilisation and possible starvation.

qs.stem: If a process can be forcibly deprived of a resource without invalidating its work, allowing preemption can break:
qs.correct: no-preemption
qs.why: The correct answer is A: no-preemption.

qs.stem: A cycle in a resource-allocation graph proves deadlock:
qs.correct: when each resource type has one instance; with multiple instances it indicates possible deadlock
qs.why: The correct answer is A: when each resource type has one instance; with multiple instances it indicates possible deadlock.
options: when each resource type has one instance; with multiple instances it indicates possible deadlock

qs.stem: Available=(3,2), Allocation P1=(1,0), P2=(1,1), P3=(1,0), Max P1=(2,1), P2=(1,2), P3=(3,1). Which is a safe sequence?
qs.correct: P1 then P2 then P3
qs.why: The correct answer is A: P1 then P2 then P3.

openEnded.prompt: State and explain the four necessary conditions for deadlock.
openEnded.key: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait; one-sentence explanation each.

openEnded.prompt: Distinguish deadlock, starvation and livelock.
openEnded.key: deadlock: circular waiting/no progress; starvation: one waits indefinitely while system progresses; livelock: active state changes but no useful progress.

openEnded.prompt: Explain prevention, avoidance, detection/recovery and the trade-off of each.
openEnded.key: prevention structurally breaks condition; avoidance uses future maximum claims/safe state; detection permits then finds; recovery preemption/rollback/termination; overhead vs utilisation.

openEnded.prompt: Run Banker’s algorithm on a supplied Allocation/Max/Available table, either approve or reject a request, and justify the result.
openEnded.key: compute Need=Max−Allocation; simulate Work/Finish; safe sequence; then compare request to Need/Available; only commit if post-request state remains safe.

title: Real-time operating systems
source: SC2005 lecture slides, tutorial material, lab manuals and quiz screenshots.
context: Real-time operating systems: practise both conceptual explanations and exam-style traces/calculations.

qs.stem: A hard real-time task must:
qs.correct: meet its deadline or the result may be invalid
qs.why: The correct answer is A: meet its deadline or the result may be invalid.
options: meet its deadline or the result may be invalid

qs.stem: An example of a real-time control system is:
qs.correct: airbag control
qs.why: The correct answer is A: airbag control.

qs.stem: A deadline is:
qs.correct: the latest acceptable completion time
qs.why: The correct answer is A: the latest acceptable completion time.

qs.stem: RTOS design prioritises:
qs.correct: predictable timing
qs.why: The correct answer is A: predictable timing.

qs.stem: A sensor interrupt is generated by:
qs.correct: an external/device event
qs.why: The correct answer is A: an external/device event.

qs.stem: In a hard real-time system, average response time is insufficient because:
qs.correct: a single missed deadline may be unacceptable
qs.why: The correct answer is A: a single missed deadline may be unacceptable.
options: a single missed deadline may be unacceptable

qs.stem: A soft real-time task generally:
qs.correct: benefits from timely completion but tolerates occasional lateness
qs.why: The correct answer is A: benefits from timely completion but tolerates occasional lateness.
options: benefits from timely completion but tolerates occasional lateness

qs.stem: To improve predictability, an RTOS may avoid:
qs.correct: unbounded blocking and unpredictable paging
qs.why: The correct answer is A: unbounded blocking and unpredictable paging.

qs.stem: Priority inversion occurs when:
qs.correct: a high-priority task waits for a resource held by a low-priority task, while medium-priority work delays release
qs.why: The correct answer is A: a high-priority task waits for a resource held by a low-priority task, while medium-priority work delays release.
options: a high-priority task waits for a resource held by a low-priority task, while medium-priority work delays release

qs.stem: A timer is useful in RTOS scheduling because it:
qs.correct: provides a predictable preemption/deadline reference
qs.why: The correct answer is A: provides a predictable preemption/deadline reference.

qs.stem: A feasible schedule requires each task to complete:
qs.correct: by its deadline under the assumed execution and release constraints
qs.why: The correct answer is A: by its deadline under the assumed execution and release constraints.
options: by its deadline under the assumed execution and release constraints

qs.stem: A long nonpreemptible critical section is dangerous in RTOS because it can:
qs.correct: delay a higher-priority task past its deadline
qs.why: The correct answer is A: delay a higher-priority task past its deadline.
options: delay a higher-priority task past its deadline
reduce all memory use to zero

qs.stem: Priority inheritance addresses priority inversion by:
qs.correct: temporarily raising the resource holder’s priority
qs.why: The correct answer is A: temporarily raising the resource holder’s priority.
options: temporarily raising the resource holder’s priority

qs.stem: A periodic task with period T and deadline D needs analysis of:
qs.correct: worst-case execution time, release/period and deadline
qs.why: The correct answer is A: worst-case execution time, release/period and deadline.
options: worst-case execution time, release/period and deadline

qs.stem: An RTOS may sacrifice average throughput to:
qs.correct: guarantee bounded response and deadline behaviour
qs.why: The correct answer is A: guarantee bounded response and deadline behaviour.
options: guarantee bounded response and deadline behaviour

qs.stem: A high-priority control task is released every 10 ms, has WCET 3 ms, and can be blocked for 8 ms by a lower-priority task; a medium task is always ready. Which design issue is most urgent?
qs.correct: priority inversion and blocking analysis may make the 10 ms deadline infeasible; use bounded critical sections/protocols
qs.why: The correct answer is A: priority inversion and blocking analysis may make the 10 ms deadline infeasible; use bounded critical sections/protocols.
options: priority inversion and blocking analysis may make the 10 ms deadline infeasible; use bounded critical sections/protocols

openEnded.prompt: Distinguish hard and soft real-time systems with one example each.
openEnded.key: hard deadline miss unacceptable; soft late result degrades service; examples airbag vs multimedia playback.

openEnded.prompt: Explain why predictability is often more important than peak throughput in an RTOS.
openEnded.key: deadlines; worst-case rather than average; bounded interrupt/scheduling/locking delays; safety/correctness consequences.

openEnded.prompt: Explain priority inversion and two ways to mitigate it.
openEnded.key: low-priority holder blocks high priority; medium task preempts holder; priority inheritance/ceiling; bound critical sections and blocking.

openEnded.prompt: Given periodic tasks with release times, WCETs and deadlines, construct or reject a priority schedule and identify the first missed deadline.
openEnded.key: timeline; account for preemption, blocking and interrupt overhead; justify feasibility, not just average utilisation.

title: Virtualization
source: SC2005 lecture slides, tutorial material, lab manuals and quiz screenshots.
context: Virtualization: practise both conceptual explanations and exam-style traces/calculations.

qs.stem: A virtual machine is an isolated duplicate of a:
qs.correct: real machine/system
